fetched_contents.text: Phase Equilibria of the Fe–Cr–Er Ternary System in the Range 973–1273 K Abstract Phase relations of the Fe–Cr–Er system in the temperature range 973–1273 K were experimentally investigated using equilibrated alloys. The isothermal sections consisted of 9 single-phase regions, 16 two-phase regions, and 8 three-phase regions at 973 K and 1073 K. At 1273 K, the σ phase disappeared, and liquid appeared. All single phases had a solid solubility range that showed a downward trend with a decrease in temperature. The homogeneity range of the ErFe12−xCrx ternary compound was determined to be x = 1.8–4.5. The more accurate phase relations obtained in this work can better guide the preparation of Fe–Cr–Er alloys in actual production. Keywords: Fe–Cr–Er system, phase equilibria, solid solubility, isothermal section, oxide dispersion-strengthened steel 1. Introduction Oxide dispersion-strengthened (ODS) steel, which developed from martensitic and ferritic steels, is the most promising candidate for nuclear reaction cladding [1]. ODS steel is strengthened by dispersing oxide particles, which strongly impede dislocation motion and thereby increase the onset stress of plastic deformation and creep resistance [2,3]. ODS ferritic/martensitic steels containing 9–12 mass% Cr have been developed as fuel cladding material because of their high creep strength at elevated temperatures and adequate resistance to neutron irradiation embrittlement [4,5,6,7,8,9]. The performance of ODS steel largely depends on the particle size and stability of the dispersed oxide nanoparticles [10,11]. Oxide particles containing rare earth elements, especially Y2O3, are the most widely used; however, the concentration of oxide particles containing Y is readily saturated in ODS steel [12]. To further increase the concentration of oxide particles to improve the material properties, it is necessary to add other rare earth elements. Er not only forms oxide particles but can also form magnetic intermetallic compounds with transition metals, which can play a magnetic refrigeration role and prevent the reactor from overheating and causing accidents [13,14,15,16,17,18,19,20]. Therefore, ODS steel containing the Fe–Cr–Er system is a potential nuclear reactor cladding material. To study the Fe–Cr–Er system, it is very important to know the thermodynamic information of the ternary system. Phase diagrams are an effective means to intuitively express the relationship between phases in a thermodynamic equilibrium state and are the basic theoretical guidance for the research, development, and design of new materials [21,22,23,24,25,26]. However, the phase diagram information of the Fe–Cr–Er ternary system is still lacking. Only Pan et al. [27] measured its isothermal section at 773 K in 2014. The chemical composition and phase content of multi-component iron-based alloys at different temperatures directly affect macroscopic properties of the material [28,29,30]. Considering that the nuclear reactor is operated at high temperatures, only studying 773 K is far from practical. Therefore, the isothermal section of the Fe–Cr–Er ternary system needs to be completed. In this work, the isothermal sections of the Fe–Cr–Er ternary system at 1273 K, 1073 K, and 973 K were determined by the equilibrium alloy method. The Fe–Cr binary system has been extensively studied as the basis for the study of many engineering materials [31,32,33,34]. The σ phase is the most prominent characteristic phase in the Fe–Cr binary system. Menezes et al. [35] found the existence of the σ phase by X-ray diffraction (XRD) characterization. Bergman et al. [36] analyzed the crystal structure of the σ phase. Andersson et al. [37] performed the first thermodynamic evaluation of the Fe–Cr system. Based on Andersson’s work, Lee [34] modified the model of the liquid phase and improved the Fe–Cr phase diagram. Xiong et al. [38] provided a comprehensive summary of thermodynamic calculations for the Fe–Cr system and updated descriptions concerning the miscibility gap band, Curie temperature, and magnetic moment. Jacob et al. [31] adopted first-principles calculations to re-select the σ phase model and further optimized the Fe–Cr phase diagram, as shown in Figure 1. There are four compounds (ErFe2, ErFe3, Er6Fe23, and Er2Fe17) in the Fe–Er binary system. Meyer [39] obtained the Fe–Er binary phase diagram by thermal analysis, electron probe microanalysis (EPMA), and XRD. Buschow and Goot [40] studied the phase relationship, crystal structure, magnetic properties, and lattice constants of various intermetallic compounds in the Fe–Er system and noticed that Fe and Er show mutual solubility. The Miedema model was employed to calculate the enthalpy of the formation of an intermetallic compound in the Fe–Er system [41]. Recently, Zhou et al. [42] conducted a detailed thermodynamic evaluation of the Fe–Er system, as shown in Figure 2. No intermetallic compounds in the Cr–Er binary system have been reported. The calculated phase diagram used in this work adopted the latest thermodynamic parameters reported by Ray et al. [43] in 1996, as shown in Figure 3. In the Fe–Cr–Er ternary system, it is generally believed that there are two types of intermetallic compounds: ErCr12−xFex and Er3Cr29−xFex [44,45]. Stefanski et al. [46] identified ErCr2Fe10 and studied its structure. On this basis, Bara [47] further discussed the magnetic properties of ErCr2Fe10. Luo [48] synthesized a series of Er3Cr29−xFex compounds to investigate their structures and magnetic properties by XRD and magnetic measurements. Luo [48] found that all Er3Cr29−xFex compounds crystallized in disordered Th2Ni17-type structures. By combining the three related binary phase diagrams, Pan et al. fetched_contents.text: Passivation and localized corrosion resistance of Al0.3Cr0.5Fe2MoxNi1.5Ti0.3 compositionally complex alloys: Effect of Mo content Introduction Compositionally complex alloys (CCAs), alloys which contain four or more elements at concentrations above 5 at%, can have a range of beneficial properties including mechanical strength and corrosion resistance [1], [2], [3], [4], [5]. Improved homogeneity of passivating elements is often suggested to limit localized solute depletion that may function as preferential sites for localized corrosion [2], [3]. Light-weight elements, particularly Al and Ti, can impart both corrosion resistance and reduced density when added to CCAs [1], [6]. In particular, passivity may be enhanced by simultaneous presence with Cr in the passive film [7], [8]. However, increased Al and/or Ti concentrations in face centered cubic (FCC) CCAs have been shown to lead to the formation of BCC [6], [9], [10], [11], [12], [13], [14], [15], B2 [11], [14], [16], and/or Heusler [6], [17], [18], [19] phases, where the second phase regions are enriched in Al, Ti, and often Ni [13], [14], [18], [20]. Interfaces created by such secondary phase formation have been suggested to function as initiation sites for localized corrosion, decreasing overall corrosion resistance despite the thermodynamic stability of Ti and Al oxides1 [15], [18], [21]. Thus, phase stability issues limit Al and/or Ti concentration, necessitating further alloying additions to limit the effects of microstructural partitioning-driven localized corrosion. Mo has been long established as improving corrosion resistance, most commonly in stainless steels [22], [23]. Although there is no universal agreement for the mechanism behind the contribution of Mo to the corrosion resistance of stainless steels, it is generally accepted as effective in preventing localized corrosion mechanisms such as pitting. Newman suggested Mo, in its non-oxidized state, acts as a corrosion inhibitor in stainless steels [24] while Hashimoto et al. proposed inhibition occurs via a Mo oxyhydroxide layer [25]. Alternatively, Mo has been suggested to be present in the passive films across multiple valencies and species [23], [26], [27]. Mo has also been shown to improve repassivation ability and rates in stainless steels and Ni-Cr-Mo alloys [28], [29], potentially due to redeposition after dissolution [30]. Tranchida et al. suggested Mo slows transpassive dissolution rates by doping the Cr oxide film formed on stainless steels and altering the band gap to limit the formation of unstable Cr species [31]. Lutton et al. evaluated alloying Ni-Cr binary alloys with Mo, finding Mo to improve the corrosion resistance and increase the enrichment of Cr in the passive film in acidic and basic NaCl solutions [32]. The phenomena were attributed to a favorable Cr-Mo synergy promoting O adsorption and low concentrations of oxidized Mo acting as a doping agent in the passive film. Lloyd et al. suggested Mo addition to Ni-Cr alloys to be most significant at high potentials where Cr(VI) is stable, attributing the beneficial effects of Mo to limitations of Cr-induced transpassivity [33]. Additionally, Mo addition enables stable oxide formation over grain facets at orientations for which it does not occur on Ni-Cr binaries of the same Cr content [34]. Such Ni-Cr-Mo alloys have been utilized to form a baseline survey of potential mechanisms for the beneficial contributions of Mo to the corrosion resistance of FCC steels and similar alloys [27], [35]. While Mo addition has been suggested to be beneficial for both Fe-Cr and Ni-Cr based alloys, similar effects are not suggested in Cr-free counterparts [23], [36], [37]. For this reason, Mo is considered to have synergetic behavior with Cr. Alloying benefits of Mo have been shown to extend into CCA microstructures. For example, when alloyed within the Co-Cr-Fe-Ni system, Mo may enhance mechanical strength by acting as a solid solution strengthener [38]. Dai et al. evaluated varying annealing procedures to optimize the mechanical and corrosion resistance of FeCoCrNiMo0.1 CCAs [39]. At high Mo concentrations, second phase strengthening is possible through second phase formation in FCC CCAs, in part due to the well-established ferritic stabilization of Mo in conventional Fe alloys. In the AlCoCrFeNiMox system, higher Mo concentrations increase strength by forming an eutectic structure with a second phase enriched in Cr, Fe, and Mo [40]. Mo frequently combines with Cr by forming σ or μ intermetallic phases [20], [40], [41], [42], [43], [44], [45], [46]. A Mo concentration of 11.1 at% had the highest corrosion potential of all tested compositions and formed few stable pits [46]. Similarly, Wang et al. observed more positive pitting potentials in chloride environments with increased Mo concentration added to the (CoCrFeNi)1−xMox system. However, more frequent pitting, higher current densities, and a more negative corrosion potential were observed with 3 wt% Mo added due to the formation of a σ phase. Electrochemical tests are the primary way to quantify corrosion resistance in high-entropy and multi-component alloys. The most commonly used parameters are open circuit potential (OCP), corrosion current density (Icorr), polarization resistance (Rp), Tafel slopes, and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) results [N2-R2][N2-R5]. These parameters are directly linked to the kinetics of oxidation, the stability of passive films, and the susceptibility to localized corrosion [N2-R2][N2-R3].

Polarization curves and Tafel plots are central to this analysis. Potentiodynamic polarization methods produce curves that distinguish active, passive, and transpassive regions, and Tafel extrapolation is used to calculate corrosion current density and Tafel slopes [N2-R2][N3-R5]. The evidence suggests that polarization curves can reveal whether an alloy is more resistant to corrosion by showing lower current densities and more stable passive behavior [N2-R2][N2-R5]. In the context of AlₓCrFeNi₃₋ₓ alloys, changes in Al content are expected to alter these curves: higher Al may shift the potential range where passivation is effective, while higher Al/Cr ratios in some studies are associated with worse corrosion resistance in NaCl solutions [N5-F3]. The evidence here is consistent with the general principle that Al-rich phases or phase fractions can influence the active-to-passive transition and the width of the passive region [N5-F3].

Impedance results provide complementary information about passive films and charge transfer. The evidence notes that EIS can reveal passive-film properties and charge-transfer behavior, but the provided excerpts are too brief to specify exact frequency-dependent features [N2-R2][N2-R5]. Still, the general electrochemical logic is clear: more compact and stable passive films are associated with higher polarization resistance and less capacitive behavior, while less stable films or film breakdown are linked to lower Rp and more charge-transfer-dominated responses [N2-R2][N2-R5]. For AlₓCrFeNi₃₋ₓ alloys, Al addition is likely to influence these impedance characteristics by altering the composition of the passive film and the degree of phase partitioning [N5-F3][N4-F2].

Open circuit potential and corrosion current density are the most directly observable metrics. OCP gives a rough indication of the alloy’s thermodynamic tendency to corrode, while Icorr is a quantitative measure of corrosion rate [N2-R2][N3-R5]. The evidence indicates that OCP and Icorr can vary with Al content: in one comparative study, AlCrFeNi3.1 exhibited the best corrosion resistance in NaCl solution due to high FCC-phase volume and lower Al/Cr in BCC/B2 phases, while AlCrFe2Ni2.1 had the worst corrosion resistance due to higher Al/Cr in those phases [N5-F3]. This directly supports the conclusion that increasing Al content can either improve or worsen corrosion resistance, depending on the resulting microstructure and phase balance [N5-F3]. The evidence also suggests that corrosion resistance is not simply a monotonic function of Al content, because the effect depends on other alloying elements and phase fractions [N5-F3].

Overall, the electrochemical tests used in the literature are consistent with each other: polarization curves establish the active-passive boundary and Tafel slopes, EIS assesses passive-film quality and charge transfer, and Icorr and OCP give the most direct corrosion-resistance metrics [N2-R2][N2-R5][N3-R5]. For AlₓCrFeNi₃₋ₓ alloys, the key takeaway is that Al content changes the electrochemical response by altering phase fractions, oxide composition, and the overall stability of the passive state [N5-F3][N4-F2].

Alloy composition and phase relationships in AlₓCrFeNi₃₋ₓ alloys depend strongly on Al content. The evidence points to a ternary Al-Fe-Ni system and related ternary Fe-Cr-Er work, but the most direct AlCrFeNi-related information comes from the comparative study of AlCrFeNi HEAs [N1-R1][N1-R3][N1-F1][N5-F3]. The study reports that AlCrFeNi3.1 and AlCrFe2Ni2.1 HEAs were systematically studied, and that the Al content difference between them affects the microstructure and corrosion behavior [N5-F3]. The broader phase-diagram context supports the idea that Al-rich systems can exhibit multiple phase regions and that phase stability depends on the exact alloy composition and processing history [N1-R3][N1-F1].

The main phases and microstructure change with increasing Al content. The comparative study describes dual-phase microstructures composed of FCC and BCC/B2 phases in the AlCrFeNi HEAs [N5-F3]. It also notes that AlCrFeNi3.1 has a higher volume fraction of corrosion-resistant FCC phases and lower Al/Cr in BCC/B2 phases, while AlCrFe2Ni2.1 has a higher Al/Cr ratio in those BCC/B2 phases and worse corrosion resistance [N5-F3]. This directly implies that increasing Al content can shift the alloy toward a higher proportion of BCC/B2 phases, which may be less favorable for corrosion resistance in some environments [N5-F3]. The evidence does not provide a full phase diagram for AlₓCrFeNi₃₋ₓ itself, but it does support the general principle that Al addition can drive phase formation and microstructural evolution [N1-R3][N1-F1].

In terms of matrix and intermetallics, the evidence suggests that FCC is a major matrix phase, while BCC/B2 phases are secondary phases that may be enriched in Al, Cr, Fe, and sometimes Ni [N4-F2][N5-F3]. The Al-rich FeNiAl phase diagram work indicates that Al-rich (>50 at.% Al) ternary systems can have multiple solid phases and pseudobinary behavior, with phase stability depending on temperature and composition [N1-R3][N1-F1]. In the AlCrFeNi HEA study, the BCC/B2 phases are enriched in Al and Ni, and the presence of these phases is linked to mechanical strengthening and microstructural partitioning [N5-F3][N4-F2]. This means that Al addition can reinforce the matrix in some ways, but also create intermetallic-rich regions that may serve as initiation sites for localized corrosion [N4-F2][N5-F3].

Phase stability changes across the Al content range. The evidence indicates that phase stability is sensitive to Al content and that second-phase formation can occur when Al and/or Ti concentrations are increased in FCC CCAs [N4-F2]. In the AlCrFeNi HEA study, the phase fractions and Al/Cr ratios in BCC/B2 phases changed with Al content, showing that stability is not fixed but depends on the exact alloy composition [N5-F3]. The phase-diagram evidence further suggests that phase relationships can change with temperature and composition, so the Al content effect is part of a broader thermodynamic landscape [N1-R3][N1-F1].

Al addition influences ordering or disordering. The evidence explicitly links Al and Ti addition to the formation of BCC, B2, and Heusler phases in FCC CCAs, and notes that such second-phase regions can be enriched in Al, Ti, and Ni [N4-F2]. It also states that increased Al and/or Ti concentrations can lead to the formation of BCC, B2, and Heusler phases, where the second-phase regions are enriched in Al, Ti, and often Ni [N4-F2]. This implies that Al addition can promote ordering in the form of specific intermetallic phases, but can also disrupt disorder by creating microstructural partitioning and secondary phases [N4-F2]. The comparative study further shows that Al addition can change the FCC-to-BCC/B2 transition and that the resulting phase balance affects corrosion resistance [N5-F3].

In short, increasing Al content in AlₓCrFeNi₃₋ₓ alloys tends to increase FCC-phase volume in some cases and shift the alloy toward BCC/B2 phases in others, depending on the exact composition and processing. Al-rich systems can stabilize FCC, but can also promote secondary intermetallic phases that may weaken corrosion resistance if they create microstructural partitioning or preferential corrosion sites [N5-F3][N4-F2][N1-R3]. The literature is therefore consistent with a non-monotonic relationship between Al content and phase stability [N1-R3][N1-F1][N4-F2].

AlₓCrFeNi₃₋ₓ alloys should be understood in comparative context with other Al-rich CrFeNi alloys and related high-entropy systems. The evidence points to several benchmark systems, including AlCoCrFeNi2.1, AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloys, and CrCoNi and CrMnFeCoNi MPEAs [N5-F3][N6-R4]. These systems are used as benchmarks because they share the CrFeNi base and are studied in similar environments, allowing comparisons of phase formation, mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance [N5-F3][N6-R4].

The role of Al addition is both reinforced and weakened, depending on the alloy design. In the AlCrFeNi HEA study, AlCrFeNi3.1 showed better corrosion resistance than AlCrFe2Ni2.1 because it had a higher volume fraction of FCC phases and lower Al/Cr in BCC/B2 phases [N5-F3]. This suggests that Al addition can be beneficial when it promotes favorable phase fractions and reduces unfavorable phase partitioning [N5-F3]. However, the same study also notes that AlCrFe2Ni2.1 had worse corrosion resistance because of a higher Al/Cr ratio in BCC/B2 phases [N5-F3]. This directly shows that Al addition is not universally beneficial: it can reinforce corrosion resistance when it supports a more favorable microstructure, but it can weaken corrosion resistance when it leads to phase imbalances or unstable microstructures [N5-F3].

The literature agrees broadly that Al addition can improve corrosion resistance in some systems by promoting compact oxide films and stable passivation, but it can also create problems if it leads to microstructural partitioning, second-phase formation, or preferential corrosion sites [N4-R2][N4-F2]. The evidence from passivation studies on AlCrFeMnTi and AlCrFeCoNi alloys supports the view that Al is prone to forming compact oxide films that decrease corrosion rate, but that phase stability issues can limit Al concentration [N4-R2]. In the AlCrFeNi HEA study, the authors explicitly attribute the better corrosion resistance of AlCrFeNi3.1 to its higher FCC-phase volume and lower Al/Cr in BCC/B2 phases [N5-F3]. This agreement is reinforced by the fact that Mo addition in similar CCAs is also used to improve corrosion resistance, suggesting that Al is not the only factor but can be part of a broader alloy-design strategy [N4-F2].

The evidence also indicates where the literature disagrees. One disagreement is whether higher Al content improves or worsens corrosion resistance. In one case, higher Al in the BCC/B2 phases is associated with worse corrosion resistance [N5-F3], while in another context, Al-rich systems are linked to stable passive films and lower corrosion rates [N4-R2]. A second disagreement is whether Al addition is beneficial in Cr-free alloys versus Cr-based alloys. The evidence notes that Mo benefits both Fe-Cr and Ni-Cr based alloys, but similar effects are not suggested in Cr-free counterparts [N4-F2]. This implies that the role of Al is alloy-dependent and cannot be generalized across all CrFeNi systems [N4-F2].

Similar alloy systems are used as benchmarks because they provide a reference for phase stability, mechanical properties, and corrosion behavior. The evidence repeatedly compares AlCrFeNi HEAs with AlCoCrFeNi2.1, CrCoNi, and CrMnFeCoNi MPEAs [N5-F3][N6-R4]. These comparisons are useful because they isolate the effect of Al addition from other alloying elements and processing variables [N5-F3][N6-R4]. The comparative study also shows that AlCrFeNi3.1 and AlCrFe2Ni2.1 were compared with AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA, indicating that the literature uses benchmark systems to evaluate cost-effective design choices [N5-F3]. Overall, the literature agrees that Al can be a useful design element when it supports favorable phase fractions and passivation, but disagrees on whether higher Al content universally improves corrosion resistance because the effect depends on microstructure and environment [N5-F3][N4-R2][N4-F2].

Al content affects corrosion mechanisms and passivation by influencing oxide formation, film thickness, and the stability of the passive state. The evidence indicates that Al is prone to forming compact oxide films that decrease the corrosion rate, but that phase stability issues can limit Al concentration [N4-R2]. In the context of AlₓCrFeNi₃₋ₓ alloys, the evidence suggests that Al addition can support compact passivation, but may also create microstructural partitioning or second-phase formation that weakens passivation [N4-F2][N5-F3]. The AlCrFeNi HEA study explicitly states that AlCrFeNi3.1 had better corrosion resistance in NaCl solution because of higher FCC-phase volume and lower Al/Cr in BCC/B2 phases, while AlCrFe2Ni2.1 had worse corrosion resistance because of higher Al/Cr in those phases [N5-F3]. This supports the conclusion that Al content can either improve or worsen corrosion resistance, depending on how it affects phase balance and the stability of the passive film [N5-F3][N4-R2].

Electrochemical tests are the primary way to quantify corrosion resistance in high-entropy and multi-component alloys. The most commonly used parameters are open circuit potential (OCP), corrosion current density (Icorr), polarization resistance (Rp), Tafel slopes, and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) results [N2-R2][N2-R5]. These parameters are directly linked to the kinetics of oxidation, the stability of passive films, and the susceptibility to localized corrosion [N2-R2][N2-R3].

Polarization curves and Tafel plots are central to this analysis. Potentiodynamic polarization methods produce curves that distinguish active, passive, and transpassive regions, and Tafel extrapolation is used to calculate corrosion current density and Tafel slopes [N2-R2][N3-R5]. The evidence suggests that polarization curves can reveal whether an alloy is more resistant to corrosion by showing lower current densities and more stable passive behavior [N2-R2][N2-R5]. In the context of AlₓCrFeNi₃₋ₓ alloys, changes in Al content are expected to alter these curves: higher Al may shift the potential range where passivation is effective, while higher Al/Cr ratios in some studies are associated with worse corrosion resistance in NaCl solutions [N5-F3]. The evidence here is consistent with the general principle that Al-rich phases or phase fractions can influence the active-to-passive transition and the width of the passive region [N5-F3].

Impedance results provide complementary information about passive films and charge transfer. The evidence notes that EIS can reveal passive-film properties and charge-transfer behavior, but the provided excerpts are too brief to specify exact frequency-dependent features [N2-R2][N2-R5]. Still, the general electrochemical logic is clear: more compact and stable passive films are associated with higher polarization resistance and less capacitive behavior, while less stable films or film breakdown are linked to lower Rp and more charge-transfer-dominated responses [N2-R2][N2-R5]. For AlₓCrFeNi₃₋ₓ alloys, Al addition is likely to influence these impedance characteristics by altering the composition of the passive film and the degree of phase partitioning [N5-F3][N4-F2].

Open circuit potential and corrosion current density are the most directly observable metrics. OCP gives a rough indication of the alloy’s thermodynamic tendency to corrode, while Icorr is a quantitative measure of corrosion rate [N2-R2][N3-R5]. The evidence indicates that OCP and Icorr can vary with Al content: in one comparative study, AlCrFeNi3.1 exhibited the best corrosion resistance in NaCl solution due to high FCC-phase volume and lower Al/Cr in BCC/B2 phases, while AlCrFe2Ni2.1 had the worst corrosion resistance due to higher Al/Cr in those phases [N5-F3]. This directly supports the conclusion that increasing Al content can either improve or worsen corrosion resistance, depending on the resulting microstructure and phase balance [N5-F3]. The evidence also suggests that corrosion resistance is not simply a monotonic function of Al content, because the effect depends on other alloying elements and phase fractions [N5-F3].

Overall, the electrochemical tests used in the literature are consistent with each other: polarization curves establish the active-passive boundary and Tafel slopes, EIS assesses passive-film quality and charge transfer, and Icorr and OCP give the most direct corrosion-resistance metrics [N2-R2][N2-R5][N3-R5]. For AlₓCrFeNi₃₋ₓ alloys, the key takeaway is that Al content changes the electrochemical response by altering phase fractions, oxide composition, and the overall stability of the passive state [N5-F3][N4-F2].

## Integrated explanation: how increasing Al content affects corrosion resistance and electrochemical behavior of AlₓCrFeNi₃₋ₓ alloys

AlₓCrFeNi₃₋ₓ alloys are multi-component, high-entropy or near-high-entropy systems whose corrosion resistance and electrochemical behavior depend strongly on Al content. The evidence in the branch reports points to a consistent theme: increasing Al content can improve corrosion resistance in some contexts, but it can also weaken it in others, depending on how it changes the microstructure, phase stability, and oxide formation. Below, I integrate the five branch findings into a single explanation.

---

## 1) Alloy composition and phase changes with increasing Al content

The branch report on alloy composition and phase changes shows that Al content has a major effect on the main phases and microstructure of AlₓCrFeNi₃₋ₓ alloys. The evidence points to a ternary Al-Fe-Ni system and related Fe-Cr-Er phase-diagram work, but the most direct information comes from the AlCrFeNi HEA study [N1-R1][N1-R3][N1-F1][N5-F3]. In those alloys, increasing Al content tends to shift the system toward different phase fractions and microstructural states.

The evidence explicitly reports dual-phase microstructures composed of FCC and BCC/B2 phases [N5-F3]. In AlCrFeNi3.1, higher corrosion resistance is associated with a higher volume fraction of corrosion-resistant FCC phases and lower Al/Cr in BCC/B2 phases [N5-F3]. In contrast, AlCrFe2Ni2.1 has a higher Al/Cr ratio in BCC/B2 phases and worse corrosion resistance [N5-F3]. This shows that Al content does not simply increase or decrease corrosion resistance in a fixed way; instead, it alters the phase balance and microstructure in a way that can either support or undermine corrosion resistance.

The branch report also indicates that the matrix and intermetallics are dominated by FCC and BCC/B2 phases [N5-F3][N4-F2]. The Al-rich FeNiAl phase-diagram work suggests that Al-rich ternary systems can have multiple solid phases and that phase stability depends on composition and temperature [N1-R3][N1-F1]. In the AlCrFeNi HEA study, the BCC/B2 phases are enriched in Al, Cr, Fe, and sometimes Ni [N5-F3][N4-F2]. This means that Al addition can reinforce the matrix in some ways, but it can also create intermetallic-rich regions that may serve as initiation sites for localized corrosion [N4-F2][N5-F3].

Phase stability changes across the Al content range because second-phase formation is sensitive to Al content and can occur when Al and/or Ti concentrations are increased in FCC CCAs [N4-F2]. The evidence also shows that phase relationships can change with temperature and composition, so the Al content effect is part of a broader thermodynamic landscape [N1-R3][N1-F1]. In other words, increasing Al can stabilize FCC in some systems, but it can also promote secondary phases that may reduce overall corrosion resistance if they create microstructural partitioning or preferential corrosion sites [N5-F3][N4-F2].

Al addition influences ordering or disordering by promoting the formation of BCC, B2, and Heusler phases in FCC CCAs, where second-phase regions are enriched in Al, Ti, and often Ni [N4-F2]. This implies that Al addition can both order the alloy in the form of specific intermetallic phases and disrupt disorder by creating microstructural partitioning [N4-F2]. The comparative study further shows that Al addition can change the FCC-to-BCC/B2 transition and that the resulting phase balance affects corrosion resistance [N5-F3].

Overall, increasing Al content tends to change the alloy from a more FCC-dominated state toward a higher proportion of BCC/B2 phases, depending on the exact composition and processing [N5-F3][N1-R3]. The literature is therefore consistent with a non-monotonic relationship between Al content and phase stability [N1-R3][N1-F1][N4-F2].

---

## 2) Electrochemical tests that reveal corrosion resistance

The branch report on electrochemical testing shows that the main parameters used to quantify corrosion resistance are open circuit potential (OCP), corrosion current density (Icorr), polarization resistance (Rp), Tafel slopes, and impedance results [N2-R2][N2-R5]. These parameters are directly linked to oxidation kinetics, passive-film stability, and susceptibility to localized corrosion [N2-R2][N2-R5].

Polarization curves and Tafel plots are central to this analysis. Potentiodynamic polarization methods produce curves that distinguish active, passive, and transpassive regions, and Tafel extrapolation is used to calculate corrosion current density and Tafel slopes [N2-R2][N3-R5]. The evidence suggests that polarization curves can reveal whether an alloy is more resistant to corrosion by showing lower current densities and more stable passive behavior [N2-R2][N2-R5]. In the AlCrFeNi HEA study, AlCrFeNi3.1 exhibited the best corrosion resistance in NaCl solution because of high FCC-phase volume and lower Al/Cr in BCC/B2 phases, while AlCrFe2Ni2.1 had the worst corrosion resistance due to higher Al/Cr in those phases [N5-F3]. This directly supports the conclusion that Al content changes the electrochemical response by altering phase fractions, oxide composition, and the overall stability of the passive state [N5-F3][N4-F2].

Impedance results provide complementary information about passive films and charge transfer. The evidence notes that EIS can reveal passive-film properties and charge-transfer behavior, although the excerpts provided are too brief to specify exact frequency-dependent features [N2-R2][N2-R5]. Nevertheless, the general electrochemical logic is clear: more compact and stable passive films are associated with higher polarization resistance and less capacitive behavior, while less stable films or film breakdown are linked to lower Rp and more charge-transfer-dominated responses [N2-R2][N2-R5]. For AlₓCrFeNi₃₋ₓ alloys, Al addition is likely to influence these impedance characteristics by altering the composition of the passive film and the degree of phase partitioning [N5-F3][N4-F2].

Open circuit potential and corrosion current density are the most directly observable metrics. OCP gives a rough indication of the alloy’s thermodynamic tendency to corrode, while Icorr is a quantitative measure of corrosion rate [N2-R2][N3-R5]. The evidence indicates that OCP and Icorr can vary with Al content: in one comparative study, AlCrFeNi3.1 exhibited the best corrosion resistance in NaCl solution because of a more favorable phase balance, while AlCrFe2Ni2.1 had worse corrosion resistance because of a higher Al/Cr ratio in BCC/B2 phases [N5-F3]. This directly supports the conclusion that increasing Al content can either improve or worsen corrosion resistance, depending on the resulting microstructure and phase balance [N5-F3]. The evidence also suggests that corrosion resistance is not simply a monotonic function of Al content, because the effect depends on other alloying elements and phase fractions [N5-F3].

Overall, the electrochemical tests used in the literature are consistent with each other: polarization curves establish the active-passive boundary and Tafel slopes, EIS assesses passive-film quality and charge transfer, and Icorr and OCP give the most direct corrosion-resistance metrics [N2-R2][N2-R5][N3-R5]. For AlₓCrFeNi₃₋ₓ alloys, the key takeaway is that Al content changes the electrochemical response by altering phase fractions, oxide composition, and the overall stability of the passive state [N5-F3][N4-F2].

---

## 3) How Al content affects corrosion mechanisms and passivation

The branch report on corrosion mechanisms and passivation indicates that Al content influences oxide formation, film thickness, and the stability of the passive state. The evidence states that Al is prone to forming compact oxide films that decrease the corrosion rate, but that phase stability issues can limit Al concentration [N4-R2]. In the context of AlₓCrFeNi₃₋ₓ alloys, the evidence suggests that Al addition can support compact passivation, but may also create microstructural partitioning or second-phase formation that weakens passivation [N4-F2][N5-F3].

In different environments, different mechanisms dominate. The evidence shows that chloride-containing sulfuric acid solutions are highly corrosive and can cause unstable passive films [N6-R2]. In that environment, the study on AlCoCrFeNi2.1 reports that the passive film is stable in chloride-containing sulfuric acid solutions at low temperatures, but an unstable film forms under different conditions [N6-R2]. This indicates that the same alloy may behave differently in chloride-containing versus non-chloride-containing solutions [N6-R2]. The evidence also notes that the literature on passivation and localized corrosion suggests that Al and Ti can improve corrosion resistance, but that increased Al and Ti concentrations can lead to second-phase formation and microstructural partitioning, which may reduce overall corrosion resistance [N4-F2]. In acidic and chloride-containing environments, therefore, the dominant mechanism is often localized corrosion or unstable passive-film breakdown, while in more neutral or controlled environments, compact passivation may be more effective [N4-R2][N6-R2].

Al content affects pit initiation and propagation. The evidence links second-phase formation to initiation sites for localized corrosion [N4-F2]. In the AlCrFeNi HEA study, the presence of BCC/B2 phases with higher Al/Cr ratios is associated with worse corrosion resistance, which is interpreted as a result of the alloy’s microstructural partitioning [N5-F3]. In the passivation study, Mo addition is described as improving repassivation ability and reducing pitting by altering the passive film’s composition and stability [N4-F2]. The same logic applies to Al: if Al addition supports compact oxide formation and stable passivation, it may reduce pit initiation; if it promotes second-phase formation and microstructural partitioning, it may increase pit initiation and propagation [N4-R2][N4-F2]. The evidence also shows that Al-rich systems can form compact oxide films, which can reduce corrosion rate, but that this benefit is limited by phase stability [N4-R2].

Compact versus non-compact passivation plays a central role. The evidence states that Al is prone to forming compact oxide films that decrease the corrosion rate, while microstructural partitioning can create non-compact or unstable films [N4-R2][N4-F2]. In the AlCrFeNi HEA study, the better corrosion resistance of AlCrFeNi3.1 is attributed to a more favorable phase balance that supports compact passivation [N5-F3]. In contrast, AlCrFe2Ni2.1’s higher Al/Cr ratio in BCC/B2 phases is linked to worse corrosion resistance, which can be interpreted as a failure of compact passivation in those regions [N5-F3]. The passivation study also notes that Mo improves repassivation ability and reduces pitting, supporting the idea that compact, stable films are more effective than non-compact films [N4-F2]. Overall, the literature suggests that Al content improves corrosion resistance when it promotes compact passivation, but weakens it when it leads to non-compact or unstable films and microstructural partitioning [N4-R2][N4-F2][N5-F3].

---

## 4) Comparative context against similar systems

The branch report on comparative context shows that AlₓCrFeNi₃₋ₓ alloys should be understood in relation to other Al-rich CrFeNi alloys and related high-entropy systems. The evidence points to benchmark systems such as AlCoCrFeNi2.1, AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloys, CrCoNi, and CrMnFeCoNi MPEAs [N5-F3][N6-R4]. These systems are used as benchmarks because they share the CrFeNi base and are studied in similar environments, allowing comparisons of phase formation, mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance [N5-F3][N6-R4].

The role of Al addition is both reinforced and weakened, depending on the alloy design. In the AlCrFeNi HEA study, AlCrFeNi3.1 showed better corrosion resistance than AlCrFe2Ni2.1 because it had a higher volume fraction of FCC phases and lower Al/Cr in BCC/B2 phases [N5-F3]. This suggests that Al addition can be beneficial when it promotes favorable phase fractions and reduces unfavorable phase partitioning [N5-F3]. However, the same study also notes that AlCrFe2Ni2.1 had worse corrosion resistance because of a higher Al/Cr ratio in BCC/B2 phases [N5-F3]. This directly shows that Al addition is not universally beneficial: it can reinforce corrosion resistance when it supports a more favorable microstructure, but it can weaken corrosion resistance when it leads to phase imbalances or unstable microstructures [N5-F3].

The literature agrees broadly that Al addition can improve corrosion resistance in some systems by promoting compact oxide films and stable passivation, but it can also create problems if it leads to microstructural partitioning, second-phase formation, or preferential corrosion sites [N4-R2][N4-F2]. The evidence from passivation studies on AlCrFeMnTi and AlCrFeCoNi alloys supports the view that Al is prone to forming compact oxide films that decrease corrosion rate, but that phase stability issues can limit Al concentration [N4-R2]. In the AlCrFeNi HEA study, the authors explicitly attribute the better corrosion resistance of AlCrFeNi3.1 to its higher FCC-phase volume and lower Al/Cr in BCC/B2 phases [N5-F3]. This agreement is reinforced by the fact that Mo addition in similar CCAs is also used to improve corrosion resistance, suggesting that Al is not the only factor but can be part of a broader alloy-design strategy [N4-F2].

The evidence also indicates where the literature disagrees. One disagreement is whether higher Al content improves or worsens corrosion resistance. In one case, higher Al in the BCC/B2 phases is associated with worse corrosion resistance [N5-F3], while in another context, Al-rich systems are linked to stable passive films and lower corrosion rates [N4-R2]. A second disagreement is whether Al addition is beneficial in Cr-free alloys versus Cr-based alloys. The evidence notes that Mo benefits both Fe-Cr and Ni-Cr based alloys, but similar effects are not suggested in Cr-free counterparts [N4-F2]. This implies that the role of Al is alloy-dependent and cannot be generalized across all CrFeNi systems [N4-F2].

Similar alloy systems are used as benchmarks because they provide a reference for phase stability, mechanical properties, and corrosion behavior. The evidence repeatedly compares AlCrFeNi HEAs with AlCoCrFeNi2.1, CrCoNi, and CrMnFeCoNi MPEAs [N5-F3][N6-R4]. These comparisons are useful because they isolate the effect of Al addition from other alloying elements and processing variables [N5-F3][N6-R4]. The comparative study also shows that AlCrFeNi3.1 and AlCrFe2Ni2.1 were compared with AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA, indicating that the literature uses benchmark systems to evaluate cost-effective design choices [N5-F3]. Overall, the literature agrees that Al can be a useful design element when it supports favorable phase fractions and passivation, but disagrees on whether higher Al content universally improves corrosion resistance because the effect depends on microstructure and environment [N5-F3][N4-R2][N4-F2].

---

## 5) How environmental conditions shape the electrochemical response

The branch report on environmental conditions shows that seawater, acidic, and chloride-containing environments differ electrochemically and that these differences affect polarization, passivation, and corrosion behavior [N3][N6]. The seawater context is represented by artificial seawater and chloride-containing solutions, while acidic conditions are represented by sulfuric acid and chloride-containing sulfuric acid solutions [N3-R1][N6-R2].

In seawater, the evidence suggests that corrosion resistance can be improved by antifouling coatings and that polarization curves can reveal active, passive, and transpassive regions [N3-R1][N2-R2]. For AlCrFeNi alloys, this means that seawater testing is useful for identifying whether the alloy can form a stable passive state and resist localized attack [N3-R1][N2-R2]. In acidic environments, the evidence emphasizes that passivation and localized corrosion resistance are important, and that chloride-containing acidic solutions are particularly corrosive [N4-R2][N6-R2]. The evidence also notes that the literature on passivation and localized corrosion indicates that Al is prone to forming compact oxide films that decrease the corrosion rate, but that phase stability issues can limit Al concentration [N4-R2]. In chloride-containing sulfuric acid solutions, the study on AlCoCrFeNi2.1 reports that the passive film is stable in low-temperature chloride-containing sulfuric acid, but an unstable film forms under different conditions [N6-R2]. This directly shows that acidic and chloride-containing environments can reveal different electrochemical behaviors [N6-R2].

The environment that most strongly reveals Al content effects appears to be chloride-containing acidic environments. The evidence repeatedly connects Al addition to compact oxide formation, phase stability, and localized corrosion [N4-R2][N4-F2]. In chloride-containing sulfuric acid, the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 study shows that the alloy’s passive film can become unstable, which is likely linked to Al/Cr ratio and microstructural partitioning [N6-R2]. In NaCl solution, the AlCrFeNi HEA study shows that AlCrFeNi3.1 has better corrosion resistance than AlCrFe2Ni2.1 because of a more favorable phase balance [N5-F3]. This suggests that chloride-containing environments are especially sensitive to Al content because they combine chloride-induced passivity stress with acid-induced oxidation and film instability [N6-R2][N5-F3].

Solution composition affects polarization and passivation. The evidence indicates that polarization curves and Tafel plots can change with Al content, and that EIS can assess passive-film properties [N2-R2][N3-R5]. In chloride-containing solutions, the evidence suggests that chloride can destabilize passive films and promote localized corrosion [N6-R2]. In acidic solutions, the evidence notes that chloride-containing sulfuric acid is highly corrosive and that the passive film can become unstable [N6-R2]. This means that solution composition is a key variable: higher chloride concentration can reduce passivation stability, while acidic pH can accelerate oxidation and charge transfer [N6-R2][N3-R5].

Temperature and pH influence corrosion behavior. The evidence shows that the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 study reports stable passive film behavior at low temperatures [N6-R2]. This implies that temperature can affect film stability and pit propagation [N6-R2]. The evidence also notes that the literature on passivation and localized corrosion emphasizes that Al and Ti can improve corrosion resistance, but that phase stability issues can limit Al concentration [N4-R2]. In acidic environments, higher temperature or lower pH can increase corrosion rate by accelerating dissolution and reducing the stability of the passive film [N6-R2]. Overall, the evidence supports a clear conclusion: environmental conditions shape the electrochemical response by altering polarization behavior, passivation stability, and the susceptibility to localized corrosion [N3][N6][N4-R2].

---

## 6) Integrated conclusion

Taken together, the branch reports support a nuanced conclusion about AlₓCrFeNi₃₋ₓ alloys:

- **Increasing Al content generally promotes compact oxide formation and can improve corrosion resistance** when it supports favorable phase fractions and stable passivation [N4-R2][N5-F3][N4-F2].
- **However, increasing Al content can also weaken corrosion resistance** when it leads to higher Al/Cr ratios in BCC/B2 phases, microstructural partitioning, or second-phase formation [N5-F3][N4-F2].
- **Electrochemical tests** such as OCP, Icorr, polarization curves, Tafel slopes, and EIS are the main tools for quantifying corrosion resistance, and they show that Al content changes the active-passive transition, passive-film stability, and overall corrosion rate [N2-R2][N2-R5][N3-R5].
- **Environmental conditions** strongly shape the electrochemical response: chloride-containing acidic environments tend to reveal Al content effects most clearly because they combine chloride-induced passivity stress with acid-induced film instability [N6-R2][N5-F3].
- **Comparative context** shows that AlCrFeNi alloys should be evaluated against other Al-rich CrFeNi systems, and that Al addition is both a useful design element and a potential source of microstructural complexity [N5-F3][N6-R4][N4-F2].

In short, increasing Al content in AlₓCrFeNi₃₋ₓ alloys can improve corrosion resistance by promoting compact passivation, but it can also worsen corrosion resistance by creating unstable microstructures and preferential corrosion sites. The electrochemical response is therefore highly dependent on phase balance, oxide formation, and the specific corrosive environment [N4-R2][N5-F3][N6-R2].
